prompt: A hash has a 160-bit digest. By the birthday bound, about how many bits of collision resistance can it offer at best?
Somebody says SHA-256 "has no collisions". What is the accurate statement?

choices.text: SHA-256 has no collisions because its output is long
choices.why: Any function to a fixed length has collisions.

choices.text: SHA-256 collisions are common but harmless
choices.why: None has ever been found.

choices.text: Collisions exist, but none has ever been found
choices.why: Right: the promise is about finding.

choices.text: Collisions only exist for inputs over 2^64 bytes
choices.why: They exist at every length beyond 256 bits.

prompt: Match each hash to its digest size.
Why did NIST standardise SHA-3 although SHA-2 had not been broken?
hint: SHA-1 and SHA-2 share a construction.

choices.text: Because SHA-2 was too slow for modern processors
choices.why: Speed was not the motive.

choices.text: As a spare built on a different design
choices.why: Right: if SHA-2 falls, the next standard is ready.

choices.text: Because SHA-2 has the length-extension weakness that breaks signatures
choices.why: Length extension does not affect signatures.

choices.text: To replace SHA-2 in TLS by 2020
choices.why: SHA-2 is still the default in TLS.

prompt: A developer builds a request check as SHA-256(secret + body). Which property of SHA-256 makes that unsafe?

choices.text: Its collisions, which let the body be swapped
choices.why: No SHA-256 collision is known.

choices.text: Its 256-bit output, too short for a secret
choices.why: 256 bits is plenty.

choices.text: The avalanche effect
choices.why: The avalanche effect is a strength.

choices.text: Length extension
choices.why: Right: the body can be extended without the secret; use HMAC, lesson 6.

prompt: What did researchers learn to do that broke MD5 and SHA-1?

choices.text: Find collisions quickly

choices.text: Recover the key used to compute the digest
choices.why: A hash has no key.

choices.text: Make the digest shorter than its declared size
choices.why: The size is fixed by the algorithm.

prompt: Why does a hash collision let a signature on one document count for another?

choices.text: Because the collision also reveals the private key
choices.why: The key stays secret; it is not needed.

choices.text: Because both documents are encrypted with the same key
choices.why: Signing does not encrypt.

choices.text: The signature covers the digest, which both share
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because signatures expire when a hash is deprecated
choices.why: Nothing expires; the forgery is mathematical.
